items.title: Ann Rabson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 21, 2007
items.q: I never got to see him live. Never. But he was live on the radio.

ctx.x: all. But sometimes I will — I don’t listen to music like I used to before I became so involved in it. I mean I really just don’t. But I do, like at festivals I get to hear other people and sometimes I’ll go out and hear other people. My life right now, I have people at home I take care of. My mother-in-law lives with me and my mother is close by. And so I don’t go out as much as I did or will in the future sometime. I mean I certainly plan to spend more time listening to other people. But I love hearing live…
There’s that Big Bill Broonzy moment all over again.

Yeah. Oh absolutely. And you know I never got to see him live. Never. But he was live on the radio. You know? It was almost. And there are a lot of people I regret. I mean there’s this jazz piano player I heard on the radio once when I shouldn’t have been listening to the radio. A guy named Gene Harris. And I thought wow, that’s really great. I’m going to go see him. So I wrote his record company and I said could you tell me where he’s going to be? Would you put me on his mailing list. I’ve got all these frequent…

items.title: Ann Rabson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 21, 2007
items.q: I heard Big Bill Broonzy playing live on the radio... And it really changed my life.

ctx.x: I was four years old and I heard live on the radio, a college radio, Purdue’s radio station, I heard Big Bill Broonzy playing live on the radio. And I was just blown away. I mean I’d heard lots of music in my home, but it was like this was my music. It was like, and he was singing, you know looking back I know, one of the songs he sang was “I’m Going to Move Way Out on the Outskirts of Town.” And I know that as a kid you can’t really understanding the sort of sexual innuendo and all that. But what came through to…
